newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German industry in bid to break tax deadlock.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German industry in bid to break tax deadlock.

text.p: Germany's industry lobby weighed into a national tax reform debate on Monday by proposing firms should pay tax on wages for unsocial work hours but attacking coalition plans to claw back windfall company profits.

The president of the Federation of German Industry (BDI), Hans-Olaf Henkel, met Finance Minister Theo Waigel last week and suggested that firms pay 10 percent tax on night, Sunday and holiday shifts while workers pay nothing, BDI spokesman Dieter Rath said.
He told Reuters the BDI's proposal would prevent a further rise in job-killing welfare costs -- which at over 40 percent of pay are among the highest in Europe.
If the tax relief was scrapped, "we would also have to fear...that trade unions would seek higher compensation at the next pay round," Rath said.

Government plans to end tax breaks on shift work have been rejected by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD). Germany's biggest trade unions have said they would protest and petition against the move.
Even Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber, a leader of Waigel's own Christian Social Union (CSU), said at the weekend he opposed taxing shift work.
"Here we are simply losing confidence...so that we cannot push through the basic reforms we must make," he told ZDF public television.
The issue is a major stumbling block in coalition-SPD talks aimed at reaching a deal by Easter to cut corporate and income tax while scrapping over 70 tax breaks.

A third round of tax reform talks is planned on Saturday, and SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine on Monday repeated his demand for a big cut in occupational insurance schemes this summer to go hand-in-hand with tax cuts.
"High labour overheads are the main structural problem of the German economy. Here we must offer a big reduction to workers and companies," Lafontaine told a news conference.
The coalition wants to cut taxes by 30 billion marks ($17.7 billion) a year by 1999 to fight record post-war unemployment and put the German economy on track for European monetary union (EMU).
Rath said the extra sum brought into federal coffers through the 10 percent tax payment on shift work would be "not insignificant", but did not put a figure on the amount.
The BDI proposal met with a cautious response, with the Finance Ministry saying that no agreements had been reached to deviate from the coalition's agreed tax position.

But Wolfgang Gerhardt, leader of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said the idea was worth discussing. SPD chief Lafontaine said industry and labour leaders should discuss it before it is taken up by politicians in Bonn.

The BDI also welcomed the cross-party consensus on cutting the main corporate tax rate to 35 from 47 percent. But it was outraged by government plans to claim backtax on extraordinary earnings from January 1, 1997 and to retroactively tax gains in the value of company assets in a bid to flush out hidden profits.
The earliest such changes should take effect would be when the measure is approved by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet, Rath said.
Despite the BDI opposing some elements of the tax reform plans it backed the overall project even though company tax bills would probably not fall at the end of the day.
"If we don't manage to complete the tax reforms, that would be a devastating signal to investors, and especially foreign investors," Rath said.
